title.en: Granular aggregate versus a rigid heap

summary: Compare a rigid authored heap with a contact-by-contact particle example while allowing declared continuum, heightfield or hybrid alternatives; a sculpted mound alone does not establish granular flow.
objective: Compare a declared rigid display heap with a discrete grain example whose deliberately unsupported grains can respond to gravity and contacts.
applies_when: Sand, gravel, grain, rubble or pellets occupy a mound, hopper or hourglass.
The viewer might read a static mesh as flowing aggregate.
intent_signals: pile of gravel that I can dig
sand that should flow through a hopper
is this mound just a mesh
example_prompts: Build a hopper of spheres that jam and unjam as contacts form, labelled as a distinct-element sketch.
Sculpt a dune as a rigid mesh and state that it will not avalanche.
negative_signals: A noisy displacement map on a dune claiming to be granular flow.
A single rigid body with a sand material.
not_for: Continuum soil plasticity, fluidised beds or measured angle-of-repose certification from a mesh.
Claims beyond the DEM abstract: force-law details were not read from the full paper.

principles: This comparison selects rigid display and discrete grains; continuum, evolving heightfield and hybrid models remain valid alternatives when labeled.
The distinct-element idea owns particle motion and contacts individually. The abstract supports this concept, not a particular force law or calibrated heap slope.
Removing one buried grain need not rearrange its neighbors: redundant support or an arch may remain. Use a known unsupported configuration to inspect response.
implementation: Rigid display: own a mesh or heightfield and declare whether edits rebuild its geometry. Decorative instances alone do not provide interactive granular mechanics.

Discrete example: own grain shape/mass, position/orientation, linear/angular velocity, gravity and contact state. Select and label the solver's contact, friction and restitution policy; these authored settings are not supplied by the Cundall abstract.
A fixed bulk collider plus interactive surface grains is an allowed labeled hybrid. Keep decorative and participating grains distinguishable and avoid duplicate bulk/grain collision occupancy.
For a response check, remove the sole support of an isolated test grain in gravity, wake that grain and advance contacts. Do not demand that every removal collapse an arbitrary packing.

Pause preserves positions, orientations and velocities without advancing time. Reset restores the initial packed state, parameters and sleep flags; contacts are rebuilt consistently by the chosen solver.
observable_checks: A decorative instance removed from a rigid heap does not claim a physically derived avalanche.
The isolated grain with its sole support removed and no remaining contact accelerates under the declared gravity after waking; an unrelated stable arch may remain stationary.
Color/roughness changes leave contact parameters unchanged. Resume preserves pre-pause momentum; reset restores initial grain poses and velocities.

creative_affordances: Stylised pellets, crystals or coins can stand in for grains if contact ownership is unchanged.
A cutaway of a few force-carrying contacts is a free overlay, not a photoelastic validation.
known_limits: The Cundall and Strack claim is taken from the published abstract only; the full Géotechnique paper was not obtained, so contact-force laws and the BALL validation plots are not used here.
A few dozen spheres are an illustration of the modelling idea, not a calibrated granular material.
Authored reusable guidance; no runtime artifact has been observed for this record.

claims.statement: The distinct element method is a numerical model for assemblies of discs and spheres that uses an explicit scheme in which particle interactions are monitored contact by contact and particle motion is modelled particle by particle.
claims.scope: Abstract of Cundall and Strack, Géotechnique 29(1) 1979; full-paper force laws and photoelastic figures were not read.

source_refs.locator: Abstract: contact-by-contact interaction and particle-by-particle motion for discs and spheres
